sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.claim: National-framework source applicable to Oyo: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union and the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or public show of same-sex affection, with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the Criminal Code criminalises sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years). The twelve Shari'a-law states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — carry up to a death-penalty maximum for male same-sex conduct; Oyo is a southern state outside that regime, as the record states. The page documents that police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay ('kito') and that mass arrests recur across states (42 men arrested in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023), with no anti-discrimination protections. Supports the record's claims that the 2014 statute also reaches LGBTI organisations and that LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under the framework that applies in full to Oyo.

sources.title: The Nigerians lured into a trap and blackmailed for being gay (BBC News / BBC Africa Eye)
sources.claim: BBC Africa Eye's 15 May 2023 investigation by Ian Wafula and Tamasin Ford documents the 'kito' scheme the record warns about: criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular dating apps, entrap men, film them, and then extort, beat and even kidnap them, with the investigation interviewing 21 people about being 'kito'd'. Victims do not report to police for fear of being arrested or attacked, and the piece shows police-adjacent enforcement against the gangs, including a commander quoted as vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of police catching a kito suspect. National in scope (the underground scene described is Lagos-based), it substantiates the record's point that dating-app 'kito' extortion gangs are a nationwide risk for gay and transgender app users, a risk that applies in Oyo exactly as elsewhere in the country.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916 and that the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act — passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014 — criminalises all forms of same-sex unions, rendering any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. It states the maximum penalty under federal law is up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, and that in the southern portion of the country, which includes Akwa Ibom, the maximum punishment for same-sex sexual activity is 14 years' imprisonment. The page also records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. This is the national-framework source for the record's claim that the 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions in Akwa Ibom with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.claim: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note on Nigeria documents the national criminal framework on sexual orientation and gender identity that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. It confirms that the twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes — with penalties for same-sex conduct from lashes or caning up to death by stoning — remain in force, citing a Shari'a court in Bauchi sentencing three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, a further report of a death-by-stoning sentence from Bauchi in May 2024, and a January 2014 incident in which a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. This confirms that the death-penalty risk layer is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Akwa Ibom, which stands under the secular national 14-year framework — matching this record's position that no state-specific enforcement divergence is documented.

sources.title: Police arrest 67 gay suspects in Delta hotel - Daily Post Nigeria
sources.claim: Daily Post reports that police officers from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area of Delta State arrested 67 suspects on 27 August 2023 at 9 pm at Teebolus Hotel, Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius (the groom), 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo (the bride), 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a male cross-dresser's confession that he was a member of a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival but 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution, and that one suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. This is a direct, dated, on-the-ground record of enforcement action inside Delta State (Warri), evidencing that the national anti-LGBT framework is actively enforced in this jurisdiction and that incidents are frequently framed together with drug allegations.

sources.claim: National-framework document for Rivers State: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal and criminalises registering, operating or supporting gay organisations, while the Nigerian Criminal Code in the south criminalises sex between men with penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the SSMPA (passed January 2014) records that the law imposes 10 to 14 years' imprisonment on anyone who registers, operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. It documents that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the Act, including eight of the 21 young men arrested, but never charged, at a birthday party in Ibadan, and - relevant to Rivers State itself - the case of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to Port Harcourt to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there, saying he did not report it to the police. The named Port Harcourt incident and the nationwide abuse pattern substantiate the enforcement climate a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.

Kwara lies within Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers nationwide to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.

Trans-specific risk is documented nationally: a national broadcaster reported mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people as common, especially in northern states, and the 2024 beating-death of a prominent transgender creator in the capital — after an earlier stabbing she had said left her fearing for her life — shows lethal violence against visibly trans people, with an investigation announced but no accountability recorded in the sources.

No state-specific sources for Kwara survived audit, so no local divergence is claimed in either direction; as a north-central state it sits close to, though sources do not name it among, the northern states where Sharia criminal provisions can compound the national penalties.
